full_judgment: 8. This point though not raised by any of the parties in the courts below either in the trial court or in the appellate court, yet I permitted the learned advocate to argue the point. Certain facts stare on the face of the record. The land under the impugned kabala was purchased when the defendant No. I was a small boy of 7/8 years. The possession of the land has been found against the defendant. The impugned kabala has come from the custody of the plaintiff. The defendant No. 2 could not show that the rents of the disputed land have ever been paid by the defendant No. 1. The defendant No. 2 has alleged that M.R.R. being in the name of the defendant No. 1, the transfer of the land by the impugned kablala of the defendant No. 2 ought to have been held to be in good faith. He has also submitted that since the land has been allowed to remain in the name of ostensible owner, the purchase should be presumed to be in good faith. Even if presumption is attached to such purchase facts of the case clearly indicate that the transfer in favour of the defendant No. 2 was not in good faith. Moreover in the written statement though the defendant has made out a case of a bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration, no positive evidence as to his bonafide has been proved. It is in evidence that the plaintiff and defendant No. 2 resided in the same house and that plaintiff and defendant No. 2 are first contusions and it is therefore likely in all probability that the defendant No. 2 knew that the plaintiff purchased the land in the benami of his minor son. Further, the defendant No. 2 purchased the land without the title deed of his vendor and without ascertaining who paid the rents in order to indicate good faith.
